title: Three little words that run everything
goal: Master the three markers of Tagalog and their forms for people's names, and use *nasa* to say that something is located somewhere.
bekal: choose *ang*, *ng* or *sa* for a reason, not by guessing
swap the three for *si*, *ni* and *kay* before people's names
state a location with *nasa* and ask about it with *nasaan*

notes: **Nasaan asks about location.** It's used only for things or people, not for events. "Where is the class?" in the sense of where it takes place uses *saan*: *Saan ang klase?* The difference is subtle: *nasaan* asks where something is, *saan* asks where something happens.

**Nasa is its answer partner.** *Nasa mesa* (on the table), *nasa bahay* (at home), *nasa opisina* (at the office). For a person's name, *nasa* becomes *nasa kay*: *Nasa kay Ben ang susi.* For pronouns, just use the *sa* set: *nasa akin*, *nasa iyo*.
**Susi ng pinto** — here *ng* links two things: the key belonging to the door. This is the easiest use of *ng* for an English speaker, since it's the same as "door key" or "the door's key".
**Wala has two related meanings**: "there isn't" (existence) and "doesn't have" (possession). *Wala na* = it's gone; *wala akong pera* = I have no money. Unit 6 covers it fully.
**Kanina means "earlier"** — past time within the same day. For yesterday, use *kahapon*. Tagalog separates the two sharply.
**Lagi** means "always" and stands in front of its verb. Handy for beginners: *Lagi akong late* — I'm always late.
**Sandali** = "a moment". The fuller forms are *sandali lang* or *saglit lang*, used just like "just a moment" in English.
**Ayos lang** is one of the most characteristically Filipino expressions: "it's okay", "no problem", "all good". If you memorize only one mood-calmer, pick this one.
**Late na tayo** shows Taglish in the wild: the English word *late* dropped into the middle of a perfectly good Tagalog sentence. This isn't broken language, it's how Manila really talks.

grammars.title: The three markers and their forms for people's names
body: This is the framework of the whole language. Everything after this unit — verbs, questions, ownership — leans on this small table.
after: **Ang** marks what's at the center of attention in the sentence — what's being "told about". English signals this by word order and intonation; Tagalog uses one dedicated word.

**Ng** (read *nang*) does two jobs at once: it marks the owner (*bahay ng guro*) and it marks the thing or doer that's **not** in the spotlight (*kumain ng mangga*). The two jobs feel far apart, but they'll merge once you reach unit 11.
**Sa** is an all-purpose preposition: in, at, to, from, for, toward. There's no one-to-one match in English, because this single Tagalog word covers half of our prepositions.

grammars.title: Nasa — be located at
body: *Nasa* isn't a verb, though it's often translated by one. It's a fusion of *na* + *sa* and means "already at".

head: Sentence
Literal
Meaning
rows: The key is on the table.
I have the money (it's with me).

after: The opposite of *nasa* is **wala**: *Nasa bahay siya* (he's at home) → *Wala siya sa bahay* (he's not at home). Notice that *nasa* splits back into *sa* when it's negated.
Three place words you know from unit 2 work without *nasa*: *nandito* (here), *nandiyan* (there), *nandoon* (over there). Short forms: *andito*, *andiyan*, *andoon*.
For a place that's a destination rather than a location, plain *sa* is used: *Pupunta ako sa palengke* — I'm going to the market.

sections.title: When to use ng, when to use sa

blocks.text: This is the question Tagalog learners ask most, worldwide. The answer fits in one sentence: **ng for owners and things; sa for places and the person aimed at.**

head: Sentence
Marker
Why
rows: the thing eaten, not in the spotlight
origin of movement — coming from Manila
target of a feeling — afraid of dogs

blocks.text: The last row shows a pattern to memorize as is: feelings with a target use *sa*. *Takot sa aso* (afraid of dogs), *galit sa kaniya* (angry at him/her), *sanay sa init* (used to the heat).

blocks.title: When you're really unsure
items: Ask yourself: does this word answer **"whose"** or **"what"**? If so, *ng*.
Does it answer **"where"**, **"to where"** or **"to whom"**? If so, *sa*.
And is it the answer to **"who/what is being talked about"**? If so, *ang*.

blocks.text: *Bayan* has two meanings that are both alive: "town" and "homeland". The Philippine national anthem begins with *Bayang magiliw* — "beloved land". The same word exists in Malay as *bayan* in older usage — a small reminder of the shared Austronesian family.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right marker: ang, ng, sa, si, ni, kay.
Answer with nasa. Example: Nasaan ang susi? (mesa) → Nasa mesa ang susi.
Put the words in the right order.
